title: Design r/place with Multiple Canvases
followUps: Walk through exactly what happens, end to end, from an anonymous user clicking a pixel to that pixel appearing on another viewer's screen. Where is the latency spent, and where can a placement be lost?
How does a viewer who opens the flagship canvas mid-event get a consistent picture, given that pixels keep changing while the snapshot downloads?

Anyone can place pixels without an account. How do you enforce the per-user cooldown, and how do you stop one person with a script from acting like thousands of users? What does that cost legitimate users?
Most canvases are small and quiet, but one has millions of viewers. How does your design handle both without wasting resources on the quiet ones or melting on the hot one?
A moderator needs to undo a coordinated vandalism attack on part of the flagship canvas from the last 20 minutes. How does your design support that?

interviewer.approach: Strong answers separate the write path, the real-time read path, and the cold read path. Requirements: anonymous view and place; per-identity cooldown per canvas; many canvases with one very hot one; updates visible in about a second; last-write-wins per pixel is fine; history kept for timelapse and moderation. Estimates: flagship 2000x2000 with 32 colours is 4M pixels; at 5 bits (or 8) per pixel that is 2.5-4 MB raw, much smaller compressed; peak ~50k placements/s globally (~5M active placers on a 5-minute cooldown is ~17k/s; bursts higher); ~5M concurrent viewers needs ~50-100 WebSocket gateway nodes; fan-out of individual events (50k/s x 5M viewers) is impossible, so batch diffs per canvas (or per tile) every 100-250 ms. Write path: API validates an anonymous signed token (issued on first visit, bound to IP/device signals, harder to get under suspicion via proof-of-work or CAPTCHA), checks the cooldown atomically (Redis SET key NX EX 300 per token+canvas, plus coarser per-IP/subnet limits), writes the pixel to the canvas state (Redis BITFIELD per canvas, sharded by canvas id; the flagship can be split into tiles across shards), and appends the event to a durable log (Kafka partitioned by canvas/tile) that feeds history storage (Cassandra or object storage) and the fan-out service. Real-time path: a fan-out service consumes the log, coalesces per-canvas diffs on a short tick, and publishes to gateway nodes subscribed by canvas (pub/sub fan-out tree); clients only receive canvases (or tiles/viewport) they view. Cold read path: a snapshot service periodically renders each active canvas to a compressed image or binary with a sequence number and pushes it to object storage behind a CDN; clients load the snapshot, buffer live diffs from the WebSocket, then apply diffs with seq > snapshot seq. Multi-canvas: a canvas metadata service (size, palette, cooldown, owner, status, shard); quiet canvases share shards and can be evicted from memory and rebuilt from snapshot + log on demand; hot canvases get dedicated shards, tiles, and more gateway capacity. Moderation: per-token bans, region rollback by replaying the event log up to a timestamp or restoring the previous value per pixel, with an audit trail.
hints: What are the different kinds of traffic here? Who writes, who reads, and how often each?
How big is one canvas in bytes if you store just the colour index per pixel? What does that suggest about where canvas state can live?
If 50,000 pixels change per second and 5 million people are watching, what happens if you send each change to each viewer individually? How could you reduce that?
A new viewer needs the whole canvas, but it keeps changing. What could they download first, and how do they catch up without missing or double-applying updates?
Without accounts, what exactly is the 'user' that a cooldown applies to? How would you make it costly to mint many of them?
pitfalls: Storing every pixel as a row in a relational database and reading the whole canvas with a query on every page load.
Pushing every individual pixel event to every connected viewer: fan-out explodes; updates must be batched and scoped per canvas or tile.
Non-atomic cooldown checks (read-then-write), letting a user place several pixels at once by racing requests.
Treating anonymous identity as 'just use the IP address' without discussing NAT, mobile carriers, VPNs and bots, or as 'just use a cookie' without making new cookies costly.
No snapshot plus sequence-number catch-up, so new viewers either miss updates or see a torn canvas.
Designing only for the flagship canvas: provisioning dedicated resources for thousands of mostly idle canvases, or ignoring that one hot canvas needs to be partitioned.
Forgetting the durable event log, which makes history, timelapse and moderation rollback impossible.
facts: Anyone can view and place pixels without an account. Creating a canvas requires a verified community-owner account.
Up to about 10,000 canvases are active at once. Most are small (256x256 to 1000x1000) and have fewer than 100 viewers.
One flagship canvas is 2000x2000 and, during events, has about 5 million concurrent viewers.
Each canvas has a fixed palette of up to 32 colours.
Each anonymous user may place one pixel every 5 minutes per canvas by default; canvas owners can set anything from 10 seconds to 1 hour.
Peak load is about 50,000 pixel placements per second across all canvases, and about 7 million concurrent viewers in total.
A placed pixel should appear for other viewers within about 1 second (p99 under 2 seconds). Last write wins; briefly seeing slightly stale pixels is fine.
Every placement (canvas, x, y, colour, time, anonymous identity) must be kept for timelapses and moderation; the flagship's history is kept forever.
Moderators must be able to ban an anonymous identity and roll back a rectangular region to how it looked at an earlier time.
Users are global; viewers should get the initial canvas in under 2 seconds on a typical connection.
Bot networks are a known problem: during past events, scripted clients created thousands of identities to draw large images.
deepDives: Real-time fan-out to millions of viewers: batching, gateway tier, subscription by canvas or tile
Snapshot plus sequence-number catch-up for new viewers
Anonymous identity, atomic cooldowns, and bot resistance
Partitioning: many quiet canvases versus one hot canvas (tiling, shard placement, eviction)
Durable event log for history, timelapse, and moderation rollback
